title: Truncated monomial basis for an abelian restricted symmetric algebra
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of prime characteristic $p>0$. Let $V$ be any $k$-vector space and let $T:V\to V$ be additive with $T(cv)=c^pT(v)$ for $c\in k$ and $v\in V$. Write $\iota:V\to\operatorname{Sym}_k(V)$ for the canonical linear map into the symmetric algebra [lem-weil-pbc-symmetric-algebra-universal-property]. Form the commutative quotient algebra [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]
$$B(V,T)=\operatorname{Sym}_k(V)/(\iota(v)^p-\iota(Tv):v\in V),$$
and write $j:V\to B(V,T)$ for the induced linear map. For every basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of $V$, the elements
$$\prod_{i\in I}j(e_i)^{a_i},\qquad a:I\to\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\text{ of finite support},$$
form a $k$-basis of $B(V,T)$; the product for zero support is $1$. In particular $j$ is injective. No finite-dimensionality of $V$, finite generation under $T$, or perfectness of $k$ is assumed.

source.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207 (arbitrary ordered basis), specialized to the zero-bracket restricted Lie algebra with v^[p]=T(v); Lemma 14.43, printed p.294, applies precisely this basis with an arbitrary index set I.

proof.text: Put $S=\operatorname{Sym}_k(V)$ and $E_i=\iota(e_i)$. By [lem-sfb-symmetric-algebra-monomial-basis], the products $E^m$ indexed by finitely supported $m:I\to\mathbf N$ form a basis of $S$. For $d\ge0$, let $S_{\le d}$ consist of the finite linear combinations of those products with $|m|:=\sum_i m_i\le d$, and put $S_{\le-1}=0$. The equality $E^mE^n=E^{m+n}$ gives $S_{\le r}S_{\le s}\subseteq S_{\le r+s}$. Also $\iota(T e_i)\in S_{\le1}$: expand the vector $Te_i$ in its finite basis expansion and use linearity of $\iota$.

source.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207: ordinary PBW basis in the abelian case; Theorem 10.36, printed p.200.

proof.text: Set $c(v)=\iota(v)^p-\iota(Tv)$ and $c_i=c(e_i)$. Apply [lem-sfb-commuting-binomial-expansion] to commuting elements of $S$ with exponent $p$. For $0<r<p$ the integer identity $r\binom pr=p\binom{p-1}{r-1}$ implies $\binom pr=0$ in $k$, since $r$ is nonzero and invertible in the field [def-weil-field]. Thus $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$ in $S$. For a finite expansion $v=\sum_i a_i e_i$, repeated use of this equality, linearity of $\iota$, and the two assumptions on $T$ give $$c(v)=\sum_i a_i^p\bigl(E_i^p-\iota(Te_i)\bigr)=\sum_i a_i^p c_i.$$ Both inclusions now follow on generators: the ideal $J$ generated by all $c(v)$ equals the ideal generated by the $c_i$. No $p$th roots of the scalars are taken.

source.place: Definition 10.39, printed p.206; Theorem 10.40, printed p.207, first assertion about generators of the kernel, specialized to the abelian case.

proof.text: For finitely supported $a,b:I\to\mathbf N$ with $a_i<p$, define $M_{a,b}=E^a\prod_i c_i^{b_i}$ and $D=|a|+p|b|$. Expanding each $c_i=E_i^p-\iota(Te_i)$ shows $$M_{a,b}=E^{a+pb}+\text{a finite linear combination of }E^m\text{ with }|m|<D.$$ Indeed the term choosing $E_i^p$ from every factor is exactly $E^{a+pb}$. Every other term replaces at least one factor of degree $p$ by one of degree at most $1$, lowering total degree by at least $p-1\ge1$; step 1 supplies the product degree bound. Each $Te_i$ has finite support, and only finitely many indices occur in $a,b$, so every expansion here is finite even if $I$ is infinite. Coordinatewise division by $p$ gives a bijection $(a,b)\mapsto a+pb$ onto all finitely supported multiindices: remainders are $<p$, and the support of both quotient and remainder lies in that of the original multiindex.

source.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207: comparison of mixed monomials with ordinary PBW monomials; explicit finite expansion in the zero-bracket case.

proof.text: The mixed monomials $M_{a,b}$ form a basis of $S$. For spanning, induct on $|m|$. At degree zero $E^0=M_{0,0}=1$. In positive degree write $m=a+pb$ by division with remainder. The difference $E^m-M_{a,b}$ is a finite linear combination of monomials of smaller degree by step 3; apply the induction hypothesis to each. For independence take a nonzero finite linear relation among distinct $M_{a,b}$ and choose the largest value $D=|a|+p|b|$ among pairs with nonzero coefficient. After step 3 is substituted, its degree-$D$ terms are distinct ordinary monomials $E^{a+pb}$, since division with remainder is unique. All other terms have degree $<D$. Comparing coefficients in the ordinary basis [lem-sfb-symmetric-algebra-monomial-basis] forces every coefficient at the chosen largest degree to be zero, a contradiction. This argument requires a maximum of a finite set of natural numbers, never a finite-dimensional degree piece.

source.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207: expanded meaning of the mixed monomials forming a basis, using degree induction and a finite maximal-degree argument.

proof.text: The ideal $J=(c_i:i\in I)$ consists of finite sums of elements $f_i c_i$ with $f_i\in S$, because $S$ is commutative. Expand each $f_i$ in the mixed basis of step 4. The identity $M_{a,b}c_i=M_{a,b+\delta_i}$ shows that $J$ is contained in the span of mixed basis vectors with $b\ne0$. Conversely, if $b\ne0$, choose $i$ with $b_i>0$; then $M_{a,b}=M_{a,b-\delta_i}c_i\in J$. Consequently $J$ is exactly that span. The quotient map has kernel $J$ by [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Hence the images of the complementary basis vectors $M_{a,0}=E^a$ span $S/J$, and a finite linear combination of them in the kernel has all coefficients zero, by independence of the full mixed basis. These images are precisely $\prod_i j(e_i)^{a_i}$ for $a_i<p$.

source.place: Theorem 10.40, printed p.207: quotient by the central c_i; explicit coordinate proof of the quotient basis.

proof.text: Since $p\ge2$, every unit multiindex $\delta_i$ has all coordinates $<p$. The vectors $j(e_i)$ are therefore distinct members of the quotient basis. If $j(v)=0$, expand $v=\sum_i a_i e_i$ as a finite sum. Then $\sum_i a_i j(e_i)=0$, so basis independence gives $a_i=0$ for every $i$, and $v=0$. For $I=\varnothing$, step 1 gives $S=k\cdot1$, there are no $c_i$, and the quotient basis consists only of $1$; $V=0$ makes injectivity immediate. In all steps the supports, sums and products involved are finite. The coefficients of $T e_i$ may involve indices outside any initially chosen finite set, and no invariant finite-dimensional subspace or perfectness was used.

source.place: Theorem 10.40 and Corollary 10.41, printed p.207; arbitrary-index application in Lemma 14.43, printed p.294. The injectivity argument here does not need the finite-dimensional hypothesis of the corollary.
